newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin makes French welfare state more selective.
newsitem.headline: Jospin makes French welfare state more selective.

text.p: New Socialist French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has done something that his right-wing predecessors frequently talked of doing but never dared.
He has taken a first step towards making France's costly and largely indiscriminate welfare state more selective.

In a keynote policy speech to parliament on Thursday, Jospin announced that higher-income earners would no longer receive lavish family allowances, sparking immediate anger from family associations, Christian groups and white-collar trade unions.
Two-child families with gross earnings of more than 25,000 francs ($4,300) a month -- a comfortable middle-class income -- would no longer receive the tax-free 650 francs ($110) a month, he said.

After pro-family organisations protested, Labour and Social Solidarity Minister Martine Aubry hastened to explain the income threshold would be higher for bigger families. Three-child households receive 1,500 francs ($260) a month.
The measure was relatively timid. An estimated 200,000 of the 4.1 million households which receive family allowances will cease to get them, officials said. But it was a start.
The only benefit Jospin promised to increase was a one-time cash handout targeted at low-income families with school-age children, paid at the start of the academic year in September.

It will be quadrupled this year to 1,600 francs ($275) per child at an estimated unbudgeted cost of six billion francs ($1 billion) in a measure that should boost consumer spending and raise some VAT revenue.

In a 1994 study commissioned by then-conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur, economist Alain Minc and a panel of experts recommmended exactly such a shift from the principle of "equality" to the notion of "equity".

The government could no longer afford to sprinkle money equally across the whole of society and should target income support at the most needy, Minc argued in the report entitled "France in the year 2000".

The report, denounced by Jacques Chirac as the epitome of technocratic "one-track thinking" in the 1995 presidential election campaign, remained a dead letter after Chirac beat fellow Gaullist Balladur to the Elysee presidential palace.

Chirac's Gaullist prime minister, Alain Juppe, toyed with the idea of making welfare more selective but retreated after his plan to overhaul the hugely indebted health and social security system triggered a 24-day public transport strike.
After that bitter experience, prompted by his attempts to make civil servants work longer for a full pension, Juppe shrank from touching French workers' "acquired rights".
Juppe had parliament pass a bill to create private pension funds but swore they would be purely a supplement to France's pay-as-you-go public pensions for all, not an alternative.
Jospin has now said the new government will reconsider even that limited opening to private pensions, which has yet to be implemented.

"Our biggest problem in France is that we are obsessed with equality, fraternity and justice," said a senior policymaker who has served both left and right-wing governments and spoke on condition of anonymity.

"That makes it hard to arbitrate between irreconcilable aims such as full employment and a high minimum wage, shorter working hours and no loss of pay, high payroll taxes and incentives to employment," the official said.

Analysts said that if Jospin avoids a serious backlash to the family allowance restrictions, he may be emboldened to apply the equity principle more widely, for example on medical costs in the light of a higher-than-expected health fund deficit due to a revenue shortfall.
But they said his scope for reform was likely to be limited by his own grassroots Socialist and Communist supporters in the salaried middle classes. ($ = 5.823 French Francs)
